newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Dubai-based Dolphin takes flak in S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: Dubai-based Dolphin takes flak in S.Africa.

text.p: South African legislators on Thursday jumped to the defence of a controversial deal which gives the Dubai-based Dolphin Group commercial rights to nature reserves in a game-rich region.

Environmentalists have poured scorn on the deal, signed with the state-owned Mpumalanga Parks Board last November, and land claims by blacks -- who say they were deprived of territory under apartheid -- could yet derail it.
But four members of the provincial assembly of Mpumalanga who led a fact-finding mission to Kenya this month to check out Dolphin gave the multinational group the all-clear.
Declaring that the group was "highly impressed", legislator Chris MacPherson concluded that there was "absolutely no reason to question the bona fides" of Dolphin.
The reserves in question lie in the same province as South Africa's vast Kruger park. Under the development deal, Dolphin plans to inject 400 million rand ($91 million) into the project.

Criticism centres on the secrecy which allowed the deal to be signed without prior public debate, a clause apparently allowing profits to be accrued abroad, and charges that the parks board had sacrificed too much control to Dolphin.
"(We) are astounded by the seemingly clandestine way in which Mpumalanga's parks have been leased to the Dolphin Group," said Lyn Brown of the Wildlife and Environmental Society.
The group is a major player in Africa's, and particularly Kenya's, tourism and leisure industry, through its Block Hotels and United Touring Company.
Environmentalist Brown urged the South African government to intervene to clear up aspects of the deal, and added: "We do not believe the best interests of conservation have been served..."
Under the deal, Dolphin takes the commercial rights to five tourism areas in return for bankrolling the Parks Board's accumulated deficit for 50 years.
Built in is an agreement that blacks living on the borders of the reserves will be given a 20 percent share of development companies to be set up in the target areas.
But these communities could still scupper the project if land claims they have lodged against two reserves succeed.
The Dolphin Group has not commented publicly on the wrangle.
